templates.title: 2FAuth
templates.name: 2fauth
templates.description: Web app for your two-factor authentication codes, a self-hosted stand-in for Google Authenticator: add accounts by scanning or uploading their QR codes, then copy codes from any browser. Source: https://github.com/Bubka/2FAuth

env.name: TWOFAUTH_APP_KEY
env.label: App key (required)
env.description: Exactly 32 characters. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: TWOFAUTH_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the app key before you deploy (exactly 32 characters, openssl rand -hex 16 makes one), since the stack won't start without it. Keep it the same from then on, as it signs logins and encrypts your codes if you turn on encryption. Then open http://<your-host>:8200 (or whichever port you picked) and register: the first account becomes the admin. Anyone who can reach it can register after that, so once you're in, tick Disable registration under Admin panel --> Authentication (the menu under your email). Scanning a QR code with the camera and passkeys both need HTTPS, so behind plain http you'll be uploading QR screenshots and signing in with a password. Everything lives in the 2fauth-data volume, and since that's every 2FA secret you've got, back it up. Docs: docs.2fauth.app

templates.title: AFFiNE
templates.name: affine
templates.description: Workspace that mixes docs, whiteboards and databases, so a page can flip between writing and an endless canvas. Edits sync to this server as you type. Source: https://github.com/toeverything/AFFiNE

env.name: AFFINE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:3010 (or whichever port you picked). The first start takes a minute while it sets up the database, then it asks you to create the admin account, and whoever gets there first does, so do it straight away. The workspace it opens is only saved in your browser, so make a new one from the workspace menu (it goes on this server by default) and keep your docs there. In the admin panel at /admin, set the External URL under Settings --> Server to the address people actually use, or invite links point at localhost. New accounts can't invite anyone or make share links for their first 24 hours, which you can change under Settings --> Auth. Sign-ups need email (Settings --> Notification), so until then add people yourself under Accounts. Docs live in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume, uploads in affine-storage, and the server's own key in affine-config. Docs: docs.affine.pro

templates.title: Apache Answer
templates.name: apache-answer
templates.description: Question-and-answer site for a community, product forum or team knowledge base, with voting, accepted answers, tags, reputation and badges. Source: https://github.com/apache/answer

env.name: TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. The site starts on it, and you can change it later in the admin.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:9080 from the address you'll actually use, since the setup wizard saves it as the Site URL that links and uploads are built from. On the database step pick SQLite (it defaults to MySQL, which isn't there) and leave the file as /data/answer.db. The last step creates the admin, and whoever reaches the wizard first gets to, so do it straight away. Sign-ups stay open but need email verification, so new accounts can't post until you set up Admin --> Advanced --> SMTP, or close them under Advanced --> Login. The database, config and uploads all live in the volume. Docs: answer.apache.org/docs

templates.title: BentoPDF
templates.name: bentopdf
templates.description: PDF toolkit that runs in your browser, so files never leave your machine. Merge, split, compress, convert, sign and edit. Source: https://github.com/alam00000/bentopdf
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8090. There's no login and nothing to back up, since every PDF is processed in your browser rather than on the server. Converting Word, Excel or PowerPoint files needs it served over HTTPS though (or opened as localhost on the same machine), as browsers block the bit it relies on over plain http. Docs: github.com/alam00000/bentopdf

templates.title: Bytebase
templates.name: bytebase
templates.description: Database change management for teams. Plan, review and roll out schema changes to Postgres, MySQL and 20-odd other databases with a full history, or query them from a web SQL editor. Source: https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase

env.name: BYTEBASE_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: For Bytebase's own Postgres. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: BYTEBASE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the database password before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes a good one), since the stack won't start without it. Then open http://<your-host>:8093 (or whichever port you picked). That page creates the admin, and whoever reaches it first gets to, so do it straight away. Sign-ups stay open after that (new people join as members), so tick Disallow self-service signup under Settings --> General if anyone else can reach it, and set the External URL there to the address you actually use. Each time it starts, Bytebase sends the first account's email address, everyone's email domains and your SQL review rules to bytebase.com, unless you untick Participate in improvement program on that same page. When you add a database, use your host's IP rather than localhost, which is the Bytebase container itself. The free Community plan covers 20 users and 10 instances. Bytebase keeps everything in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume, and any sample instance you start in bytebase-data. Docs: docs.bytebase.com

templates.title: Cloudreve
templates.name: cloudreve
templates.description: Cloud drive for your own files, with share links, WebDAV, previews for documents, photos and video, and offline downloads. Source: https://github.com/cloudreve/cloudreve
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:5212 and sign up. The first account becomes the admin, and sign-ups stay open after that, so turn them off under Admin panel --> Settings --> User session if it's just you. Open the Admin panel from the address you'll actually use, too. It offers to save that as the Site URL, and until you say yes, download and share links point at localhost. The database, settings and every uploaded file live in the volume. Docs: docs.cloudreve.org

templates.title: CommaFeed
templates.name: commafeed
templates.description: RSS reader in the style of Google Reader, with four layouts, keyboard shortcuts for nearly everything, rules that mark entries as read, OPML import and the Fever and Google Reader APIs for mobile apps. Source: https://github.com/Athou/commafeed

env.name: QUARKUS_HTTP_AUTH_SESSION_ENCRYPTION_KEY
env.label: Session key
env.description: Keeps you logged in when it restarts. At least 16 characters, generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Leave it blank and every restart or update logs everyone out.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8082 and the first page creates the admin account. There's no setup code, so do it straight after deploying. Sign-ups are off, so the admin adds everyone else from the user menu --> Manage users. It won't subscribe to feeds on private addresses, so for one on your own network add COMMAFEED_HTTP_CLIENT_BLOCK_LOCAL_ADDRESSES=false to the environment, but only if you trust everyone using it. Mobile apps log in with your username and an API key, which you make at the bottom of Settings --> Profile, where the Fever and Google Reader addresses are too. Everything lives in the H2 database in the volume. Docs: athou.github.io/commafeed

templates.title: ConvertX
templates.name: convertx
templates.description: File converter for over a thousand formats, covering images, documents, audio, video and ebooks. Source: https://github.com/C4illin/ConvertX

env.name: HTTP_ALLOWED
env.label: Opening it over plain http?
env.description: ConvertX only sends its login cookie over HTTPS unless this is on. Switch it off once it's behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS.

env.name: TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:3000 and create your account straight away, since the first visitor gets it and sign-ups close after that. Uploads and the database live in the /app/data volume. It's a big image (LibreOffice, TeX and Calibre are all in there), so the first pull takes a while. You'll be logged out whenever the container restarts, unless you add a JWT_SECRET env var holding a long random string (openssl rand -hex 32). Docs: github.com/C4illin/ConvertX

templates.title: copyparty
templates.name: copyparty
templates.description: File server in one Python app, with resumable uploads, thumbnails, search and a music player in the browser, plus WebDAV for mounting it as a drive. Source: https://github.com/9001/copyparty

env.name: COPYPARTY_PASSWORD
env.label: Password (required)
env.description: What you'll log in with. Anything long and hard to guess, or generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16

env.name: COPYPARTY_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. Then open http://<your-host>:3923 (or whichever port you picked) and you'll land on a login box that only wants the password, no username. Logged in, you can upload, make folders, move, delete and see everything, while anyone else just gets that login box (upstream's own default is read-write for everyone). Files live in the copyparty-files volume, and the search index, thumbnails and logins live in copyparty-config. WebDAV clients connect to the same address, with any username and that password. Its switch to https button uses a certificate built into every copyparty, so it's no real protection, and a reverse proxy is the way to get proper HTTPS. Docs: github.com/9001/copyparty

templates.title: CyberChef
templates.name: cyberchef
templates.description: Web app for encoding, decoding, encrypting, compressing and picking apart data, by chaining hundreds of small operations into a recipe. Source: https://github.com/gchq/CyberChef
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8088. There's no login and nothing to back up, since every recipe runs in your browser and your data never reaches the server. Recipes live in the URL, so bookmark or share that to keep one. Docs: github.com/gchq/CyberChef/wiki

templates.title: DbGate
templates.name: dbgate
templates.description: Database manager in the browser for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite, MongoDB, Redis and more: browse and edit tables, write queries, compare schemas, draw diagrams and import or export data. Source: https://github.com/dbgate/dbgate

env.name: DBGATE_PASSWORD
env.label: Password (required)
env.description: For logging in as admin. DbGate has no login at all without one, hence required.

env.name: DBGATE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set a password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. Then open http://<your-host>:3600 (or whichever port you picked) and log in as admin. Each browser gets asked once about anonymous usage analytics, which stay off unless you say yes. Add your databases with New Connection, and use dockerhost as the server for one published on the Docker host itself. A restart logs you out, nothing else is lost. Saved connections, queries and uploads live in the dbgate-data volume. Whenever someone opens it, DbGate's server also asks dbgate.cloud for new shared scripts and a premium advert, mentioning which kinds of database you use. Docs: docs.dbgate.io

templates.title: Dolibarr
templates.name: dolibarr
templates.description: ERP and CRM for small businesses and freelancers: contacts, quotes, orders, invoices and payments, stock, projects, expense reports, HR and accounting. You switch on just the parts you need. Source: https://github.com/Dolibarr/dolibarr

env.name: DOLIBARR_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: For the admin login. No spaces. Only used on the very first start, change it in Dolibarr after that.

env.name: DOLIBARR_SECRET_KEY
env.label: Secret key (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or saved bank details, API keys and mail passwords can't be read.

env.name: DOLIBARR_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: DOLIBARR_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: DOLIBARR_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on
env.description: Like http://192.168.1.20:8480. Shared document links and links in emails point here.

templates.note: Fill in the admin password, secret key and database password before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes good secrets), since the stack won't start without them, and keep the key and database password the same when you redeploy. The first start takes a few minutes while it fills the database, so the page won't load straight away. Then open http://<your-host>:8480 (or whichever port you picked) and log in as admin with your password. It sends you to Setup first: add your company's name, country and currency (it starts in euros), then switch on the modules you want under Setup --> Modules. There are no sign-ups, you add everyone else under Users & Groups. Put the address you'll actually type in the browser in the address field too, since shared document links and links in emails use it, and they point at localhost until you do. To change it later, edit the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. To update, redeploy with the image re-pulled: it backs up the database into the documents volume and upgrades it on start. The first time the home page loads after an install or update, your browser sends Dolibarr an anonymous ping (a hashed id, versions, database type and country). Uploads, generated PDFs and backups live in the dolibarr-documents volume, add-on modules in dolibarr-custom, everything else in db-data. Docs: wiki.dolibarr.org

templates.title: Donetick
templates.name: donetick
templates.description: Chore and task tracker for households, with natural-language scheduling, assignee rotation, subtasks, points and rewards, labels, NFC tags and a calendar feed. Source: https://github.com/donetick/donetick

env.name: DT_SQLITE_PATH
env.label: Database file
env.description: Keeps the database in the data volume, so leave it as it is.

env.name: DT_SERVER_PUBLIC_HOST
env.label: Address
env.description: Where you'll open it, like http://192.168.1.10:2021. The calendar feed link is built from this.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:2021 and click Create one. Sign-ups stay open: everyone makes their own account, then asks to join your circle with the code under Settings --> Circle Settings, where you accept them. Once everyone's in, add DONETICK_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true to the container's environment. Crash reports and usage analytics stay off unless you tick them on the screen after signing up. Photo attachments and avatars need S3-compatible storage set up as their storage docs say, and uploads fail without it. The phone apps only connect over HTTPS with a real certificate, so they need a proxy in front. The SQLite database lives in the data volume, and the generated login secret and settings (selfhosted.yaml) in the config one. Docs: docs.donetick.com

templates.title: drawDB
templates.name: drawdb
templates.description: Database diagram editor for drawing entity relationships in the browser, then exporting them as SQL for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MariaDB or SQL Server, or importing an existing schema to see it. Source: https://github.com/drawdb-io/drawdb
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8098/editor. There's no login and nothing to back up on the server, since diagrams are saved in your browser's own storage, so another browser or a cleared cache starts empty. File --> Export as --> JSON keeps a copy, and File --> Import from brings it back. Plain /editor makes a fresh copy of your last diagram on every visit, so bookmark the /editor/diagrams/... address it moves you to. Share and version history need drawDB's separate backend, which isn't included. Icon fonts load from jsDelivr and cdnjs, and the home page at / pulls in tweets and a GitHub star count from outside services. Docs: drawdb-io.github.io/docs

templates.title: Easy!Appointments
templates.name: easy-appointments
templates.description: Online booking site for appointments: customers pick a service, a provider and a free slot, and you manage it all from a calendar with working hours, breaks and holidays per provider. Syncs with Google or CalDAV calendars. Source: https://github.com/alextselegidis/easyappointments

env.name: EASYAPPOINTMENTS_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Exactly what you'll type in the browser, port included and no slash at the end, like http://192.168.1.20:8580. Every page and link is built from it.

env.name: EASYAPPOINTMENTS_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: EASYAPPOINTMENTS_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Fill in the address and database password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The address has to be exactly what you'll type in the browser, like http://192.168.1.20:8580: the port you're using, and no slash at the end. Easy!Appointments builds every page and link from it, so if it's wrong the front page sends you off to that address instead, and any page you do reach has no styling and buttons that do nothing. To fix it, change the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Then open /index.php/installation on that address straight away, as whoever fills in that form first becomes the admin. Go there directly: once it's been opened, the front page says Database Migration Required until the install's done. It adds a sample service, provider and customer, so rename or delete those first. Customers book at the address itself, and you log in at /index.php/login. Nothing gets emailed until you add EASYAPPOINTMENTS_SMTP_HOST, EASYAPPOINTMENTS_SMTP_USER and EASYAPPOINTMENTS_SMTP_PASSWORD to the stack's environment variables and update the stack (plus EASYAPPOINTMENTS_SMTP_PORT if it isn't 587, and EASYAPPOINTMENTS_SMTP_SECURITY = ssl for port 465). Emails come from the company email you set at install. Everything lives in MariaDB, in the db-data volume, with logins and backups in easyappointments-storage. Docs: github.com/alextselegidis/easyappointments

templates.title: EspoCRM
templates.name: espocrm
templates.description: CRM for keeping track of customers and sales: accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities, cases, meetings and calls, with a shared calendar, email inbox, reports and a no-code entity builder. Source: https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm

env.name: ESPOCRM_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: For the admin login. Only used on the very first start, change it in EspoCRM after that.

env.name: ESPOCRM_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: ESPOCRM_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: ESPOCRM_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on
env.description: Like http://192.168.1.20:8680. Links in emails and password resets point here.

templates.note: Fill in the admin password and database password before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 16 makes a good one), since the stack won't start without them, and keep the database password the same when you redeploy. The first start takes a minute while it sets up the database. Then open http://<your-host>:8680 (or whichever port you picked) and log in as admin with your password. There are no sign-ups, you add everyone else under Administration --> Users. Put the address you'll actually type in the browser in the address field too, since links in emails and password resets use it, and they point at localhost until you do. It's set from the stack on every start, so to change it later edit the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy, rather than in Settings. Nothing gets emailed until you add an SMTP server under Administration --> Outbound Emails. The daemon container runs the scheduled jobs (fetching email, reminders, clean-up), so leave it running. The Administration page shows a news panel from espocrm.com, which gets told your version and address, and a scheduled job asks espocrm.com for the latest version. To update, redeploy with the image re-pulled and it upgrades the database on start. Uploads and settings live in the espocrm-data volume, extensions and customisations in espocrm-custom and espocrm-client-custom, and your records in db-data. Docs: docs.espocrm.com

templates.title: Etherpad
templates.name: etherpad
templates.description: Collaborative text editor where everyone types in the same document at once, with history, chat and plugins. This one runs on Postgres. Source: https://github.com/ether/etherpad

env.name: ETHERPAD_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: For the admin panel at /admin, where you sign in as admin. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32

env.name: ETHERPAD_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or Etherpad can't reach its database.

env.name: ETHERPAD_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set both passwords before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes good ones), since the stack won't start without them. Then open http://<your-host>:9001 (or whichever port you picked) and start a pad. Anyone who can reach it can create and edit pads, so keep it off the open internet or put a login in front of it. The admin panel is at /admin, user admin. Pads are stored in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume. Docs: docs.etherpad.org

templates.title: ezBookkeeping
templates.name: ezbookkeeping
templates.description: Personal finance app for logging what you spend and earn across accounts and currencies, with receipt photos, scheduled transactions and charts. Imports bank statement files, GnuCash and Firefly III, and installs on a phone like an app. Source: https://github.com/mayswind/ezbookkeeping

env.name: EZBOOKKEEPING_SECRET_KEY
env.label: Secret key (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or two-factor logins stop working.

env.name: EZBOOKKEEPING_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or ezBookkeeping can't reach its database.

env.name: EZBOOKKEEPING_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: EZBOOKKEEPING_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on
env.description: Like http://192.168.1.10:8100/. Receipt photos, profile pictures and the phone QR code all point here, so they break on any other address.

templates.note: Set both secrets before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes good ones), since the stack won't start without them, and keep them the same when you redeploy. Put the address you'll actually type in the browser in the address field too, or receipt photos won't load. Then open http://<your-host>:8100 (or whichever port you picked) and create an account. Tick Use Preset Transaction Categories on the second step, or you start with none. Every account gets its own separate books, but sign-ups stay open, so once you've made yours add EZBOOKKEEPING_SIGNUPS = false to the stack's environment variables and update the stack. Exchange rates come from the European Central Bank, and maps load from OpenStreetMap. Everything lives in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume, with receipt photos and avatars in ezbookkeeping-storage. Docs: ezbookkeeping.mayswind.net

templates.title: Firefly III
templates.name: firefly-iii
templates.description: Personal finance manager for tracking what comes in and goes out, with budgets, subscriptions, recurring transactions, rules and reports. This one runs on Postgres. Source: https://github.com/firefly-iii/firefly-iii

env.name: FIREFLY_APP_KEY
env.label: App key (required)
env.description: Exactly 32 characters. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or everyone's logged out and API tokens stop working.

env.name: FIREFLY_CRON_TOKEN
env.label: Cron token (required)
env.description: Exactly 32 characters, and not the same as the app key. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16.

env.name: FIREFLY_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or Firefly III can't reach its database.

env.name: FIREFLY_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: FIREFLY_TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. Transaction dates and the nightly cron use it.

env.name: FIREFLY_TRUSTED_PROXIES
env.label: Trusted proxies
env.description: Leave blank, unless it's behind a reverse proxy. Then set ** so Firefly III trusts the proxy's headers.

templates.note: Fill in all three secrets before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The app key and cron token must be exactly 32 characters (openssl rand -hex 16 makes one), and keep all three the same when you redeploy. Then open http://<your-host>:8092 (or whichever port you picked) and register. The first account becomes the admin and sign-ups close after it, so do it straight away. A small cron container pings Firefly III at 03:00 every night, which is what creates recurring transactions and fires subscription reminders. Transactions live in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume, and attachments in firefly-upload. Docs: docs.firefly-iii.org

templates.title: Grist
templates.name: grist
templates.description: Spreadsheet that works like a database, with typed columns, Python formulas, linked tables, charts and forms. Source: https://github.com/gristlabs/grist-core

env.name: GRIST_SESSION_SECRET
env.label: Session secret (required)
env.description: Signs everyone's login cookies. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32

env.name: GRIST_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the session secret before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. Then open http://<your-host>:8484 (or whichever port you picked). It asks for a boot key first, which Grist prints in the container's logs every time it starts (look for BOOT KEY), then an admin email, then walks you through Quick setup. Take care on its sign-in step: No authentication means anyone who can reach the port can open and edit everything, so only pick it on a private network. Sign in with getgrist.com and forwarded headers (for Authelia and the like) are the free options, and OIDC needs an activation key. The last step has product telemetry switched on, so untick it there if you'd rather it didn't. Documents, users and settings all live in the grist-data volume. Docs: support.getgrist.com/self-managed

templates.title: Halo
templates.name: halo
templates.description: Website and blogging platform with a rich editor, themes, plugins, comments and pages, run from a web console. This one runs on Postgres. Source: https://github.com/halo-dev/halo

env.name: HALO_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or Halo can't reach its database.

env.name: HALO_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: HALO_TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. Post dates on the site use it.

templates.note: Set the database password before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes a good one), since the stack won't start without it. Then open http://<your-host>:8091 (or whichever port you picked) from the address you'll actually use, since the setup page saves it as the site's External URL. That page also creates the admin, and whoever reaches it first gets to, so do it straight away. The console is at /console. The sample post, About page, menu and category it starts with are in Chinese whatever language you pick, so rename or delete them there. Posts and settings live in Postgres, in the postgres-data volume, and uploads, themes and plugins in halo-data. Docs (in Chinese): docs.halo.run

templates.title: JupyterLab
templates.name: jupyterlab
templates.description: Python notebooks in the browser for poking at data and plotting it, with a terminal alongside. It's Jupyter's scipy-notebook image, so pandas, NumPy, matplotlib and scikit-learn come installed. Source: https://github.com/jupyter/docker-stacks
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8888. It asks for a token, which is in the container's logs (the link ending /lab?token=...). Put that token and a new password into Setup a Password underneath, and you'll log in with the password from then on - otherwise the token changes on every restart. Whoever logs in gets a terminal inside the container, so keep it off the open internet unless it's behind HTTPS. Your notebooks, settings, password and anything you pip install --user live in the home folder volume. A plain pip install goes into the image and is gone after an update. Docs: jupyter-docker-stacks.readthedocs.io

templates.title: Kanboard
templates.name: kanboard
templates.description: Kanban project management that stays out of the way, with boards, swimlanes, subtasks, time tracking, automatic actions and a plugin system. Source: https://github.com/kanboard/kanboard
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8094 and sign in as admin / admin, then change that password straight away under My profile --> Change password, as it's the same on every install. There are no open sign-ups, the admin adds users. Set Settings --> Application URL to the address you use, so links in emails point to the right place. The SQLite database and attachments live in the data volume, plugins in the other. Docs: docs.kanboard.org

templates.title: Kener
templates.name: kener
templates.description: Status page with built-in monitoring: it checks your sites, APIs, ports and DNS on a schedule and shows uptime, response times, incidents and planned maintenance on a public page. Source: https://github.com/rajnandan1/kener

env.name: KENER_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Exactly what you'll type in the browser, port included and no slash at the end, like http://192.168.1.20:3700.

env.name: KENER_SECRET
env.label: Secret key (required)
env.description: Signs everyone's logins. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: KENER_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Fill in the address and secret key before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The address has to be exactly what you'll type in the browser, like http://192.168.1.20:3700: the port you're using, and no slash at the end. Kener refuses any form sent from another address, so if it's wrong the status page still shows but signing in or saving anything gives you Cross-site POST form submissions are forbidden. To fix it, change the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Then go to /account/signin straight away, as the first person there sets up the admin account. New monitors need a type under Configuration (the service URL on its own is just a link), and only show on the public status page once you add them to it under Pages. The two sample monitors check kener.ing and load their icons from there for every visitor, so delete them when you've added your own. Settings, monitors and their history live in the kener-data volume. Docs: kener.ing/docs

templates.title: KitchenOwl
templates.name: kitchenowl
templates.description: Grocery list and recipe manager for households, with shopping lists that sync live between everyone, recipes you can add to the list in one go, a meal planner and shared expenses. Source: https://github.com/TomBursch/kitchenowl

env.name: KITCHENOWL_SECRET
env.label: Secret key (required)
env.description: Signs everyone's logins. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or everyone gets logged out.

env.name: KITCHENOWL_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the secret key before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes a good one), since the stack won't start without it. Then open http://<your-host>:8070 (or whichever port you picked) and the first page creates the admin account. There's no setup code, so do it straight after deploying. Sign-ups are off, so the admin adds everyone else under Settings --> Users, then adds them to a household's members. The SQLite database and uploaded photos live in the kitchenowl-data volume. Docs: docs.kitchenowl.org

templates.title: Langflow
templates.name: langflow
templates.description: Visual builder for AI agents and workflows: drag together models, prompts, tools, vector stores and MCP servers on a canvas, chat with the result in a playground, then call it as an API or serve it as an MCP server. Source: https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow

env.name: LANGFLOW_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: For signing in as langflow. Only used to create the account on the very first start.

env.name: LANGFLOW_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Letters and numbers only, since it goes into a database URL. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32

env.name: LANGFLOW_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set both passwords before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The first start takes a couple of minutes, then open http://<your-host>:7860 (or whichever port you picked) and sign in as langflow with your admin password. Changing that password on the form later does nothing. Add your AI provider's key under Settings --> Model Providers (Ollama works too). The sign-up link makes accounts that stay locked until an admin switches them on, and the open-source version only does that through its API, so treat it as a one-person app. Any account can run its own Python on the server, so only switch on people you trust. Langflow sends anonymous usage stats to its makers. To stop it, add LANGFLOW_TELEMETRY_OFF set to true to the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Uploaded files and its generated keys live in the langflow-data volume, your flows and settings in postgres-data. Docs: docs.langflow.org

templates.title: LibreTranslate
templates.name: libretranslate
templates.description: Machine translation server with a page for translating text and documents, plus a JSON API for other apps to call. Runs its own models, so nothing you translate leaves the box. Source: https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate

env.name: LIBRETRANSLATE_LANGUAGES
env.label: Languages
env.description: Two-letter codes, comma separated, like en,es,fr,de,it,ja. Each one is a couple of hundred MB of models to download.

env.name: LIBRETRANSLATE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:5100 (or whichever port you picked). The first start downloads models for the languages you listed, about 900 MB for the default four, so give it a minute or two before the page answers. There are no accounts, so anyone who can reach it can use it and its API (reference at /docs). Keep it on your LAN, or see the docs for API keys and rate limits. To add languages later, change the list and update the stack, and the new ones download on the next start. Each start also checks for model updates. The models live in the libretranslate-models volume. Codes: supported languages. Docs: docs.libretranslate.com

templates.title: LubeLogger
templates.name: lubelogger
templates.description: Vehicle maintenance and fuel tracker: log services, repairs, fuel-ups, taxes and odometer readings for each car, attach receipts, and get reminders when something's due. Source: https://github.com/hargata/lubelog

env.name: LUBELOGGER_LOCALE_OVERRIDE
env.label: Locale
env.description: Sets the currency, number and date format, like en-GB or de-DE.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8180. There's no login out of the box, so anyone who can reach it can see and change everything until you turn one on under Settings --> Admin --> Enable Authentication, which sets up the root account. Vehicles, records, uploaded receipts and settings live in the first volume, and the second keeps everyone logged in across updates. The server checks GitHub for new versions and its sponsor list. Docs: docs.lubelogger.com

templates.title: MyIP
templates.name: myip
templates.description: IP toolbox for checking your own connection: your IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and where they look like they are, which sites you can reach, WebRTC and DNS leak tests, a speed test, and lookups for MTR, DNS records and whois. Source: https://github.com/jason5ng32/MyIP

env.name: MYIP_HOSTS
env.label: Host name or IP you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Just the host, no http:// and no port, like 192.168.1.20 or myip.example.com. For several, use commas and no spaces.

env.name: MYIP_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Fill in the host name or IP you'll open it on before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. That's just the host part of the address, like 192.168.1.20 or myip.example.com, with no http:// and no port. MyIP's server only answers lookups for pages opened on a host it knows (plus localhost), so if it's missing or wrong the page loads but your IP cards sit there loading forever. To fix it, change it in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. More than one host goes in as a list with commas and no spaces, like 192.168.1.20,myip.example.com, since a space quietly breaks the host after it. Then open http://<your-host>:18966 (or whichever port you picked). There's no login and nothing stored. Checking your connection is the whole point, so the page talks to lots of outside services: its makers' ipcheck.ing probes, IP lookup services (through the server), leak-test servers and the sites in the connectivity test. Docs: github.com/jason5ng32/MyIP

templates.title: NocoBase
templates.name: nocobase
templates.description: No-code platform for building internal tools and business apps: define your own data tables and relations, then build pages, forms, kanbans and calendars on top, with roles, permissions and workflows. Source: https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase

env.name: NOCOBASE_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: For signing in as admin@nocobase.com. Only used on the very first start.

env.name: NOCOBASE_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or NocoBase can't reach its database.

env.name: NOCOBASE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set both passwords before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The first start installs everything and takes a minute or two (the log shows a few APP_COMMANDING errors while it does, which is normal). Then open http://<your-host>:13000 (or whichever port you picked) and sign in as admin@nocobase.com with your admin password. Changing that password on the form later does nothing, so use Change password in the user menu at the top right instead. Anyone who can reach it can sign up, and new accounts see nothing until you give their role some permissions. To stop sign-ups, untick Allow to sign up under Settings --> Authentication --> basic --> Configure. Uploads and its generated keys live in the nocobase-storage volume, everything else in postgres-data. Docs: docs.nocobase.com

templates.title: NodeBB
templates.name: nodebb
templates.description: Forum software with a modern feel: categories, topics and replies that update live, chat, notifications, groups, Markdown with image uploads, and a plugin and theme library. Source: https://github.com/NodeBB/NodeBB

env.name: NODEBB_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16

templates.note: Fill in the database password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without it. Then open http://<your-host>:4567 (or whichever port you picked) straight away, as whoever finishes the installer first makes the admin account. The database is already sorted, so it only asks for the address and an admin login. Keep the address it fills in as the one you'll always open it on, since NodeBB builds its links from it. If you ever need to change it, it's the url in config.json in the nodebb-config volume. Installing takes two or three minutes while it builds, then the forum appears. Anyone who can reach it can read the forum. Sign-ups are open with no email check (change that under Admin --> Settings --> Users), and a new member's first posts wait in the post queue until you approve them. Nothing gets emailed until you set up SMTP under Admin --> Settings --> Email, and browser push notifications need HTTPS. Federation with Mastodon and friends (Admin --> Federation) is on by default, but needs a public HTTPS address to do anything. Plugins you install from the admin panel live in nodebb-modules, uploads in nodebb-uploads, and posts and users in db-data. Docs: docs.nodebb.org

templates.title: Opengist
templates.name: opengist
templates.description: Pastebin built on Git, like GitHub Gist: every snippet is a repo you can clone, push to and fork, with syntax highlighting, Markdown, embeds, search, and public, unlisted or private gists. Source: https://github.com/thomiceli/opengist
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:6157 and register. The first account becomes the admin and sign-ups stay open after it, so once everyone's in, tick Disable signup under Admin --> Configuration (invitations still work). Public gists can be read without logging in unless you tick Require login there too. Every gist is a Git repo: clone and push over http on 6157, or over SSH on 2222 once you've added a key under Settings. Anyone who adds an email gets their avatar from Gravatar, which the same admin page can turn off. Behind an HTTPS proxy, add OG_EXTERNAL_URL (like https://gist.example.com) to the container's environment so the login cookie is Secure and passkeys work. The SQLite database, every gist's repo, the search index and the generated secret key live in the volume. Docs: opengist.io

templates.title: Papra
templates.name: papra
templates.description: Document archive for receipts, contracts, payslips and all the other paperwork you need to keep: upload them, search their text (scans included), and tag them by hand or with rules, in separate organisations for home and work. Source: https://github.com/papra-hq/papra

env.name: PAPRA_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Exactly what you'll type in the browser, port included and no slash at the end, like http://192.168.1.20:1221.

env.name: PAPRA_AUTH_SECRET
env.label: Auth secret (required)
env.description: At least 32 characters. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: PAPRA_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Fill in the address and auth secret before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The address has to be exactly what you'll type in the browser, like http://192.168.1.20:1221: the port you're using, and no slash at the end. Papra only accepts logins from that address, so if it's wrong the page still loads but signing up or logging in fails with Invalid callbackURL. To fix it, change the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. The first account you make is the admin, and sign-ups stay open after that. To close them, add PAPRA_SIGNUPS set to false to the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Documents and the database live in the papra-data volume. Docs: docs.papra.app

templates.title: PlantUML Server
templates.name: plantuml-server
templates.description: Web editor and rendering server for PlantUML, turning plain-text descriptions into sequence, class, component and other diagrams as PNG, SVG or ASCII, with a link for each one you can embed in docs and wikis. Source: https://github.com/plantuml/plantuml-server
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8380. There's no login and nothing saved on the server, since each diagram is encoded into its own address, so bookmark or share the page's address to keep one. The link above the editor renders it straight into a doc or wiki, and swapping /png/ for /svg/ gives you an SVG. PNGs get cut off at 4096 pixels across while SVGs don't, so for bigger ones add PLANTUML_LIMIT_SIZE (say 16384) to the container's environment. Includes work from public web addresses, but not from local files or your own network. Docs: plantuml.com/server

templates.title: Readeck
templates.name: readeck
templates.description: Read-it-later app that saves the full text and images of web pages, with highlights, labels, collections, full-text search and e-book export. Source: https://codeberg.org/readeck/readeck
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8097 and create your account. Whoever gets there first becomes the admin, and there are no open sign-ups after that, the admin adds users under Settings --> Users. The browser extension saves pages in one click. Readeck won't fetch pages on private addresses, so links to things on your LAN save without their content. The settings, generated secret key, SQLite database and every saved page live in the volume. Docs: readeck.org

templates.title: RSSHub
templates.name: rsshub
templates.description: RSS feed maker for thousands of sites that don't have a feed of their own, like GitHub issues, news sites, forums and shops. Source: https://github.com/DIYgod/RSSHub

env.name: ACCESS_KEY
env.label: Access key
env.description: Optional. Set one and every feed url needs it, like /hackernews?key=yourkey. Leave blank and anyone who can reach it can use it.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:1200 to check it's up, then add feeds to your reader as paths on it, like /github/issue/DIYgod/RSSHub. Every route is listed in the docs. There's no login, so set an access key if it faces the internet. Nothing to back up, feeds are cached in memory. Some routes need a browser, and for those swap the image tag to chromium-bundled.

templates.title: RustFS
templates.name: rustfs
templates.description: S3-compatible object storage written in Rust, an open-source alternative to MinIO, with a web console for browsing buckets and managing users, policies and access keys. Source: https://github.com/rustfs/rustfs

env.name: RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY
env.label: Admin password (secret key, required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. To change it later, change it here and redeploy.

env.name: RUSTFS_API_PORT
env.label: Host port for the S3 API

env.name: RUSTFS_CONSOLE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web console

templates.note: Set the secret key before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. Then open the console at http://<your-host>:9011 (or whichever port you picked) and log in with the admin user as the account (admin unless you changed it) and the secret key as the key. S3 clients and SDKs go to http://<your-host>:9010, with path-style addressing and region us-east-1. Buckets start private. Rather than hand the admin's keys to other apps, make them their own user under Users. Changing the secret key on the form and redeploying changes the admin's password, and other users carry on as they were. Everything lives in the rustfs-data volume, as a single drive with no redundancy, so back it up like any other data. Docs: docs.rustfs.com

templates.title: Seerr
templates.name: seerr
templates.description: Request manager for Jellyfin, Plex and Emby, where people ask for films and shows and Sonarr and Radarr fetch them. It's the merged successor to Overseerr and Jellyseerr. Source: https://github.com/seerr-team/seerr

env.name: TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:5055 and the setup wizard walks you through connecting your media server, then Sonarr and Radarr. Settings and the request database live in the /app/config volume. Coming from Overseerr or Jellyseerr? Seerr can take over their config, see the docs for how.

templates.title: SilverBullet
templates.name: silverbullet
templates.description: Notes app for Markdown pages you can program, with two-way links, tasks, queries over everything you've written and Lua scripting for your own commands and widgets. Source: https://github.com/silverbulletmd/silverbullet
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:3300 and the setup wizard asks for an admin account, then your first space (at /notes by default). There's no setup code, so whoever gets there first owns the server - do it straight after deploying, and from the address you'll actually use, since the admin dashboard always sends you back there (change it under Admin --> Server). Over plain http on anything but localhost it runs online-only, so no offline use, local encryption or single sign-on. Put it behind an HTTPS proxy to get those back. Accounts, settings and every page (as plain Markdown files) live in the volume. This is the slim image, so if you want the Runtime API, which needs Chromium, use the latest tag instead. Docs: docs.silverbullet.md

templates.title: SiYuan
templates.name: siyuan
templates.description: Note-taking app built from blocks, so any paragraph can be linked, embedded or queried from anywhere else. Markdown, backlinks, a graph view and daily notes. Source: https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan

env.name: SIYUAN_ACCESS_AUTH_CODE
env.label: Access code (required)
env.description: What you type in to open your notes, and the only thing between them and anyone who can reach the port. Make it long, or generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16

env.name: SIYUAN_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

env.name: SIYUAN_TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. Daily notes and timestamps use it.

templates.note: Set the access code before you deploy, since the stack won't start without one. Then open http://<your-host>:6806 (or whichever port you picked) and enter it. It takes half a minute or so to start. Every note, asset and setting lives in the siyuan-workspace volume. To change the code later, just change it here and redeploy. Docs: github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan

templates.title: Snipe-IT
templates.name: snipe-it
templates.description: IT asset manager for keeping track of laptops, licences, accessories and consumables: who has what, check-outs and check-ins, audits, maintenance, depreciation and asset tag labels. Source: https://github.com/grokability/snipe-it

env.name: SNIPEIT_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Exactly what you'll type in the browser, port included and no slash at the end, like http://192.168.1.20:8300. Every page and link is built from it.

env.name: SNIPEIT_APP_KEY
env.label: App key (required)
env.description: Exactly 32 characters. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16. Keep it the same when you redeploy.

env.name: SNIPEIT_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16

env.name: SNIPEIT_TIMEZONE
env.label: Timezone
env.description: For the dates it shows, like Europe/London.

env.name: SNIPEIT_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Fill in the address, app key and database password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The address has to be exactly what you'll type in the browser, like http://192.168.1.20:8300: the port you're using, and no slash at the end. Snipe-IT builds every page, link and redirect from it, so if it's wrong the front page sends you off to that address instead, and any page you do reach has no styling and buttons that go nowhere. To fix it, change the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Then open the address straight away, as whoever finishes the setup wizard first becomes the admin. There are no sign-ups, the admin adds everyone else under Users. Nothing gets emailed until you add SNIPEIT_MAIL_HOST, SNIPEIT_MAIL_USER, SNIPEIT_MAIL_PASSWORD and SNIPEIT_MAIL_FROM (the address it sends from) to the stack's environment variables and update the stack, plus SNIPEIT_MAIL_PORT if it isn't 587. Uploads and backups live in the snipeit-data volume, everything else in db-data. Docs: snipe-it.readme.io

templates.title: Spoolman
templates.name: spoolman
templates.description: 3D printer filament tracker that keeps count of your spools, what's left on each and where they live, makes printable QR labels, and takes usage straight from Moonraker (Klipper) or OctoPrint as you print. Source: https://github.com/Donkie/Spoolman
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:7912. There's no login at all, so anyone who can reach it can see and change your spools - keep it on your own network. Add spools searches your own catalogue plus SpoolmanDB, a public list of filaments the server downloads from GitHub, so most details fill themselves in. Moonraker and the OctoPrint plugin connect to that same address. The database and its nightly backups live in the volume. The page loads its fonts from Google Fonts. Docs: github.com/Donkie/Spoolman/wiki

templates.title: Super Productivity
templates.name: super-productivity
templates.description: To-do list with timeboxing and time tracking built in, and it can pull in issues from Jira, GitHub and GitLab. Source: https://github.com/super-productivity/super-productivity
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8095. There's no login, and your tasks are saved in your browser rather than on the server, so set up sync (WebDAV, Dropbox and others) in its settings if you use more than one device. Docs: github.com/super-productivity/super-productivity

templates.title: Teable
templates.name: teable
templates.description: Spreadsheet-style database in the vein of Airtable, built on Postgres: grid, kanban, calendar, gallery and form views, file attachments, formulas, real-time collaboration and an API. Source: https://github.com/teableio/teable

env.name: TEABLE_SECRET
env.label: Secret key (required)
env.description: Signs logins and encrypts stored tokens. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32

env.name: TEABLE_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Letters and numbers only, since it goes into a database URL. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32

env.name: TEABLE_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on
env.description: Like http://192.168.1.10:3500. Invite links and profile pictures point here, so they break on any other address.

env.name: TEABLE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the secret key and database password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The first start sets up the database and takes a couple of minutes, then open http://<your-host>:3500 (or whichever port you picked). The first account you sign up becomes the admin. Anyone who can reach it can sign up after that, so once you're in, switch off Allow creating new accounts under System Admin --> Instance settings. Set the address field to wherever you'll open it, or invite links will point at localhost. Teable's image sends a small daily usage report to Teable (your instance ID, how many people are active, and a rough count of spaces and bases). To stop it, add TEABLE_TELEMETRY_OFF set to true to the stack's environment variables and redeploy. AI features and enterprise extras need a paid licence, everything else is free. Attachments live in the teable-data volume, logins in teable-cache, and your tables in postgres-data. Docs: help.teable.ai

templates.title: Termix
templates.name: termix
templates.description: SSH terminal and server manager in the browser, with saved hosts, tunnels and a file editor. Source: https://github.com/Termix-SSH/Termix
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8080 and create an account, which becomes the admin. Registration stays open after that, so switch it off in the admin settings unless you want other people signing up. Hosts, keys and the database live in the /app/data volume, and its secrets are generated there on first start. Behind a reverse proxy it needs websockets. It sends a small anonymous usage report once a day, which you can switch off in Admin Settings > Usage Statistics. Docs: docs.termix.site

templates.title: TREK
templates.name: trek
templates.description: Trip planner for working out each day of a holiday on a map, with bookings, budgets, packing lists and live editing with whoever's coming along. Source: https://github.com/liketrek/TREK

env.name: COOKIE_SECURE
env.label: Opening it over plain http?
env.description: TREK only sends its login cookie over HTTPS unless this is on. Switch it off once it's behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS.

env.name: TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. Reminders and scheduled jobs run on it.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8099 and sign in as admin@trek.local. The password's printed in the container's logs on first start (search them for First Run), and TREK makes you pick a new one straight away. Anyone who can reach it can register their own account, so switch off Password Registration under Administration --> Settings if that's not what you want. Place search asks TREK's own places.liketrek.com as well as OpenStreetMap, add a TREK_PLACES_ENABLED=false env to keep it to OpenStreetMap. The database, its encryption key and every upload live in the two volumes. Docs: github.com/liketrek/TREK/wiki

templates.title: Verdaccio
templates.name: verdaccio
templates.description: Private npm registry and caching proxy: publish your own packages to it, and install everything else through it so npmjs downloads get cached locally. Works with npm, yarn and pnpm. Source: https://github.com/verdaccio/verdaccio
templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:4873 to browse packages, and point npm at it with npm config set registry http://<your-host>:4873/. Anything it doesn't host comes from npmjs and gets cached. There's no admin: npm login --registry http://<your-host>:4873/ makes an account the first time, and any account can publish and unpublish any package. Sign-ups stay open and packages can be read without logging in, which is upstream's default and only changes in its config.yaml, so keep it on your own network. Authors with an email get their avatar from Gravatar in the web UI. Accounts, packages, the npmjs cache and the generated token secret live in the volume. Docs: verdaccio.org

templates.title: Wakapi
templates.name: wakapi
templates.description: Coding time tracker that works with the WakaTime editor plugins. Point them at your own server and get stats per project, language, editor and machine, plus badges you can put in a README. Source: https://github.com/muety/wakapi

env.name: WAKAPI_PASSWORD_SALT
env.label: Password salt (required)
env.description: Mixed into every password hash. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or nobody can log in.

env.name: WAKAPI_COOKIE_KEY
env.label: Cookie key
env.description: Keeps you logged in when it restarts. Generate one with: openssl rand -base64 32. Leave it blank and every restart logs everyone out.

env.name: WAKAPI_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set the password salt before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes a good one), since the stack won't start without it, and keep it the same when you redeploy. Then open http://<your-host>:3100 (or whichever port you picked) and sign up. The first account is the admin. Sign-ups stay open, so once you've made yours add WAKAPI_ALLOW_SIGNUP = false to the stack's environment variables and update the stack. The setup page shows the ~/.wakatime.cfg lines for your editor's WakaTime plugin, with your API key. Invite links point at localhost until you add WAKAPI_PUBLIC_URL (like http://192.168.1.10:3100) there too. The logged-out front page loads one badge image from badges.fw-web.space. Everything lives in SQLite, in the wakapi-data volume. Docs: github.com/muety/wakapi

templates.title: Wallos
templates.name: wallos
templates.description: Subscription tracker for keeping an eye on recurring bills, with stats, multiple currencies and reminders before things renew. Source: https://github.com/ellite/wallos

env.name: TZ
env.label: Timezone
env.description: Like Europe/London. Used for renewal dates and reminders.

templates.note: Open http://<your-host>:8282 and register. The first account becomes the admin, and sign-ups are closed after that. The database and any logos you upload live in the two volumes. Docs: github.com/ellite/wallos

templates.title: YOURLS
templates.name: yourls
templates.description: URL shortener you run yourself: short links on your own address with custom keywords, click stats with referrers and countries, bookmarklets and an API for making links from scripts. Source: https://github.com/YOURLS/YOURLS

env.name: YOURLS_URL
env.label: Address you'll open it on (required)
env.description: Exactly what you'll type in the browser, port included, all lowercase and no slash at the end, like http://192.168.1.20:8400. Every short link and admin page is built from it.

env.name: YOURLS_ADMIN_PASSWORD
env.label: Admin password (required)
env.description: What you'll log in to the admin area with.

env.name: YOURLS_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 16

env.name: YOURLS_COOKIE_KEY
env.label: Cookie key
env.description: Keeps you logged in, and your API signature token the same, across updates. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Left blank, both change every time it's updated.

templates.note: Fill in the address, admin password and database password before you deploy, since the stack won't start without them. The address has to be exactly what you'll type in the browser, like http://192.168.1.20:8400: the port you're using, all lowercase, and no slash at the end. YOURLS builds every short link, page and button from it, so if it's wrong /admin sends you off to that address to install, any page you do reach has no styling and won't shorten anything, and short links point at the wrong place. To fix it, change the address in the stack's environment variables and redeploy. Then open /admin on that address (the bare address just says Forbidden, that's normal), click Install YOURLS once to set up the database, and log in with the admin username and password from the form. The login lives in the stack's environment variables, so that's where you change the password. The install adds three sample links to yourls.org, delete them if you like. Short links are public, and so are their stats pages (add a + to any short link), which load their charts and site icons from Google. For scripts, use the signature token under Tools rather than your password, and set a cookie key so the token survives updates. Links and stats live in the db-data volume. Docs: yourls.org/docs

templates.title: Zipline
templates.name: zipline
templates.description: File sharing and screenshot host that works with ShareX, Flameshot and the like, with a link shortener, text pastes, folders, and files that can expire, need a password or delete themselves after so many views. Source: https://github.com/diced/zipline

env.name: ZIPLINE_SECRET
env.label: Secret (required)
env.description: At least 32 characters. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or every login and upload token stops working.

env.name: ZIPLINE_DB_PASSWORD
env.label: Database password (required)
env.description: Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it the same when you redeploy, or Zipline can't reach its database.

env.name: ZIPLINE_PORT
env.label: Host port for the web UI

templates.note: Set both secrets before you deploy (openssl rand -hex 32 makes good ones), since the stack won't start without them, and keep them the same when you redeploy. Then open http://<your-host>:3200 (or whichever port you picked) and create the first account, which becomes the super admin. There are no open sign-ups, so you add everyone else under Users. Settings, under your name in the top corner, makes ready-to-use ShareX and Flameshot configs. Links use whatever address you opened it on, and the rest of the settings (domains, HTTPS links, sign-ups, the 100 MB file limit) live in the dashboard under Server Settings. It checks GitHub for new versions, which you can switch off there under Features. Files and thumbnails live in the zipline-uploads volume, everything else in postgres-data. Docs: zipline.diced.sh
